title: Jeremiah 52:12–23
context: The narrator reports that Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, came to Jerusalem in the fifth month, burned the LORD’s house, the king’s house, and the great houses, broke down the walls, and carried away the people, leaving some of the poorest to work the vineyards and fields. The Chaldeans broke up the bronze pillars, bases, and sea and carried off the temple vessels, and the narrator recalls the size and ornament of the pillars Solomon made. The account parallels 2 Kings 25:8–17 and Jeremiah 39:8–10, with a few differences named without harmonizing, such as the day of the month in 52:12 and the height of the capital in 52:22, and both traditions read the loss of the temple soberly as shared ground: the LORD’s warnings were fulfilled, and the house that had been trusted as a guarantee was not spared (cf. 7:4, 14).

verses.text: Now in the fifth month, in the tenth day of the month, which was the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, who stood before the king of Babylon, came into Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now in the fifth month, in the tenth day of the month, which was the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar.” Arminian readers note that 2 Kings 25:8 gives the seventh day.

How the two dates relate is discussed and is not resolved here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the difference with 2 Kings 25:8 without forcing a solution.

Shared ground: both traditions read the arrival of Nebuzaradan as the decisive moment in Jerusalem’s fall, while recording the date difference plainly.

verses.text: He burned the LORD’s house, and the king’s house; and all the houses of Jerusalem, even every great house, he burned with fire.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He burned the LORD’s house, and the king’s house; and all the houses of Jerusalem, even every great house, he burned with fire.” Arminian readers note the end of the temple Solomon built.

Jeremiah had warned of this (cf. 7:14; 26:6).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the fulfillment of the warning that the temple would not protect a disobedient people.

Shared ground: both traditions read the burning with grief, agreeing that God’s presence was never a guarantee against judgment for persistent sin.

verses.text: All the army of the Chaldeans, who were with the captain of the guard, broke down all the walls of Jerusalem all around.
verses.arminianNotes:
“All the army of the Chaldeans, who were with the captain of the guard, broke down all the walls of Jerusalem all around.” Arminian readers note the city’s complete loss of defense.

The parallel is 2 Kings 25:10.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the city left exposed.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly: Jerusalem is left without walls or protection, as the prophets had warned, and later hope for rebuilding stands against this background (cf. 29:10).

verses.text: Then Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive of the poorest of the people, and the rest of the people who were left in the city, and those who fell away, who defected to the king of Babylon, and the rest of the multitude.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive of the poorest of the people, and the rest of the people who were left in the city.” Arminian readers note the deportation of many groups.

Those who defected to Babylon are also taken.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the wide scope of the exile.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the sober account of exile, naming the parallels in 39:9 and 2 Kings 25:11 without pressing small differences.

verses.text: But Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard left of the poorest of the land to be vineyard keepers and farmers.
verses.arminianNotes:
“But Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard left of the poorest of the land to be vineyard keepers and farmers.” Arminian readers note that some remain in the land.

39:10 adds that he gave them vineyards and fields.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a remnant left even in judgment.

Shared ground: both traditions note that the land is not emptied entirely, and that the poor who remain are given work to sustain life.

verses.text: The Chaldeans broke the pillars of bronze that were in the LORD’s house and the bases and the bronze sea that were in the LORD’s house in pieces, and carried all of their bronze to Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The Chaldeans broke the pillars of bronze that were in the LORD’s house and the bases and the bronze sea.” Arminian readers note that the great bronze furnishings were broken and carried to Babylon.

Jeremiah had spoken of these items in 27:19–22.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the loss of the temple’s furnishings as part of the judgment.

Shared ground: both traditions read the list as a sober record of loss, with the parallel in 2 Kings 25:13.

verses.text: They also took away the pots, the shovels, the snuffers, the basins, the spoons, and all the vessels of bronze with which they ministered.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They also took away the pots, the shovels, the snuffers, the basins, the spoons, and all the vessels of bronze with which they ministered.” Arminian readers note the end of the ordinary temple service.

The list records the loss in plain detail.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the sacrificial service as it had been practiced in Jerusalem brought to an end.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly, noting that the vessels of worship are carried away along with the people.

verses.text: The captain of the guard took away the cups, the fire pans, the basins, the pots, the lamp stands, the spoons, and the bowls; that which was of gold, as gold, and that which was of silver, as silver.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The captain of the guard took away the cups, the fire pans, the basins, the pots, the lamp stands, the spoons, and the bowls.” Arminian readers note that gold and silver items are taken as well.

The phrase “as gold” and “as silver” suggests they were taken for their value.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the temple stripped of its treasures.

Shared ground: both traditions read the list as a record of loss, and both note that the book of Ezra later reports vessels returned (cf. Ezra 1:7–11), without harmonizing the lists.

verses.text: They took the two pillars, the one sea, and the twelve bronze bulls that were under the bases, which King Solomon had made for the LORD’s house. The bronze of all these vessels was without weight.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They took the two pillars, the one sea, and the twelve bronze bulls that were under the bases, which King Solomon had made for the LORD’s house.” Arminian readers note the reference to Solomon’s work (cf. 1 Kings 7).

The bronze was “without weight.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the glory of Solomon’s temple ending.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a reminder that the work of human hands, however skilled, cannot stand against God’s judgment on persistent sin.

verses.text: As for the pillars, the height of the one pillar was eighteen cubits; and a line of twelve cubits encircled it; and its thickness was four fingers. It was hollow.
verses.arminianNotes:
“As for the pillars, the height of the one pillar was eighteen cubits; and a line of twelve cubits encircled it.” Arminian readers note that the measurements match 1 Kings 7:15.

The narrator recalls the pillars in detail.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the care taken to remember what was lost.

Shared ground: both traditions read the measurements as a lament in the form of a record, honoring what had stood in the LORD’s house.

verses.text: A capital of bronze was on it; and the height of the one capital was five cubits, with network and pomegranates on the capital all around, all of bronze. The second pillar also had the same, with pomegranates.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The height of the one capital was five cubits.” Arminian readers note that 1 Kings 7:16 also gives five cubits, while 2 Kings 25:17 gives three.

The difference is discussed and is noted here without resolution.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the difference with 2 Kings 25:17 without harmonizing.

Shared ground: both traditions record the detail plainly and agree that the main point is the loss of the temple’s adornment.

verses.text: There were ninety-six pomegranates on the sides; all the pomegranates were one hundred on the network all around.
verses.arminianNotes:
“There were ninety-six pomegranates on the sides; all the pomegranates were one hundred on the network all around.” Arminian readers note the ornamental detail.

The pomegranates adorned the capitals (cf. 1 Kings 7:20).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the beauty of the temple recalled at the moment of its loss.

Shared ground: both traditions read the detail without building symbolism on the numbers, and they let the record stand as remembrance.
